This appendix proposes an exercise on computing the position metrics
presented in @sec-03-metrics-en, applied to the class of nine students
used as the example in that chapter. It is organised in three parts:
the exercise, with the data and a table to fill in; the answers, to
check the results; and the full step-by-step solution, showing how each
value is obtained. It is advisable to try the exercise before reading
the last two parts.

## Exercise {#sec-apA-exercise-en}

The nine students of a class, identified by the letters A to I, were
asked: "Which two classmates would you like to work with on the next
group assignment?". Each student made two choices, 18 in total. The
adjacency matrix records these choices: the row shows who chooses and
the column who is chosen (@tbl-apA-matrix-en).

| Chooses ↓ / Chosen → | A | B | C | D | E | F | G | H | I |
|:--------------------:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **A** |   | 1 | 1 |   |   |   |   |   |   |
| **B** | 1 |   | 1 |   |   |   |   |   |   |
| **C** | 1 | 1 |   |   |   |   |   |   |   |
| **D** | 1 |   | 1 |   |   |   |   |   |   |
| **E** |   |   | 1 |   |   | 1 |   |   |   |
| **F** |   |   |   |   | 1 |   | 1 |   |   |
| **G** |   |   |   |   |   | 1 |   | 1 |   |
| **H** |   |   |   |   |   | 1 | 1 |   |   |
| **I** | 1 |   |   | 1 |   |   |   |   |   |

: Adjacency matrix of the class. Each row adds up to 2, because each student chose two classmates. {#tbl-apA-matrix-en}

The sociogram draws the same data as a graph (@fig-apA-sociogram-en).

![Sociogram of the class. The size of each node is proportional to the number of times the student was chosen; the colour indicates the subnetwork they belong to; double arrows represent reciprocal choices and single arrows unreciprocated ones; the magenta connections are the bridges between the two subnetworks.](../assets/images/cap03/sociograma-turma.png){#fig-apA-sociogram-en}

The calculations use the following definitions, where *n* = 9 is the
number of students, so each student has *n* − 1 = 8 classmates:

- **Choices received:** number of classmates who chose the student.
- **Contacts:** classmates connected to the student, in either
  direction. A reciprocal choice (double arrow) counts as a single
  contact.
- **Distance:** number of steps on the shortest path between two
  students, ignoring the direction of the arrows.
- **Node density** = contacts ÷ (*n* − 1) = contacts ÷ 8.
- **Betweenness** = number of pairs of classmates whose shortest path
  goes through the student ÷ 28. The 28 pairs come from 8 × 7 ÷ 2: they
  are all the pairs that can be formed with the other eight classmates.
  If a pair has two shortest paths and only one goes through the
  student, that pair counts ½.
- **Closeness** = (*n* − 1) ÷ sum of distances = 8 ÷ sum of the
  distances from the student to each of the other eight.

The task is to fill in the following table (@tbl-apA-task-en).

| Student | Choices received | Contacts | Node density | Betweenness | Closeness |
|:-------:|:----------------:|:--------:|:------------:|:-----------:|:---------:|
| A | | | | | |
| B | | | | | |
| C | | | | | |
| D | | | | | |
| E | | | | | |
| F | | | | | |
| G | | | | | |
| H | | | | | |
| I | | | | | |

: Table to fill in with the metrics of each student. {#tbl-apA-task-en}

## Answers {#sec-apA-answers-en}

The completed table gives, for each metric, the fraction and the value
rounded to two decimal places (@tbl-apA-answers-en).

| Student | Choices received | Contacts | Node density | Betweenness | Closeness |
|:-----:|:-----------:|:--------:|:--------------:|:------------------:|:-------------:|
| A | 4 | 4 | 4/8 = 0.50 | 4/28 ≈ 0.14 | 8/17 ≈ 0.47 |
| B | 2 | 2 | 2/8 = 0.25 | 0/28 = 0.00 | 8/19 ≈ 0.42 |
| C | 4 | 4 | 4/8 = 0.50 | 16.5/28 ≈ 0.59 | 8/14 ≈ 0.57 |
| D | 1 | 3 | 3/8 ≈ 0.38 | 2.5/28 ≈ 0.09 | 8/18 ≈ 0.44 |
| E | 1 | 2 | 2/8 = 0.25 | 15/28 ≈ 0.54 | 8/15 ≈ 0.53 |
| F | 3 | 3 | 3/8 ≈ 0.38 | 12/28 ≈ 0.43 | 8/18 ≈ 0.44 |
| G | 2 | 2 | 2/8 = 0.25 | 0/28 = 0.00 | 8/24 ≈ 0.33 |
| H | 1 | 2 | 2/8 = 0.25 | 0/28 = 0.00 | 8/24 ≈ 0.33 |
| I | 0 | 2 | 2/8 = 0.25 | 0/28 = 0.00 | 8/23 ≈ 0.35 |

: Answers to the exercise: position metrics of the nine students. {#tbl-apA-answers-en}

## Step-by-Step Solution {#sec-apA-solution-en}

### Step 1: choices received {#sec-apA-step1-en}

In the matrix, add up the 1s in each student's **column**. In the
sociogram, the same value is obtained by counting the arrowheads that
reach the student (@tbl-apA-received-en).

| Student | Chosen by | Choices received |
|:-----:|:-------------:|:------------------:|
| A | B, C, D, I | 4 |
| B | A, C | 2 |
| C | A, B, D, E | 4 |
| D | I | 1 |
| E | F | 1 |
| F | E, G, H | 3 |
| G | F, H | 2 |
| H | G | 1 |
| I | nobody | 0 |

: Choices received by each student. {#tbl-apA-received-en}

As a check, the choices received must add up to the total number of
choices made: 4 + 2 + 4 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 18.

### Step 2: contacts and node density {#sec-apA-step2-en}

To find a student's contacts, combine the classmates the student
chooses (their **row** in the matrix) with the classmates who choose
them (their **column**). Anyone who appears in both lists counts only
once, because a reciprocal choice is a single contact. Node density is
the number of contacts divided by 8 (@tbl-apA-contacts-en).

| Student | Chooses | Chosen by | Contacts (no repeats) | No. of contacts | Node density |
|:-------:|:-------:|:---------:|:---------------------:|:---------------:|:------------:|
| A | B, C | B, C, D, I | B, C, D, I | 4 | 4 ÷ 8 = 0.50 |
| B | A, C | A, C | A, C | 2 | 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 |
| C | A, B | A, B, D, E | A, B, D, E | 4 | 4 ÷ 8 = 0.50 |
| D | A, C | I | A, C, I | 3 | 3 ÷ 8 ≈ 0.38 |
| E | C, F | F | C, F | 2 | 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 |
| F | E, G | E, G, H | E, G, H | 3 | 3 ÷ 8 ≈ 0.38 |
| G | F, H | F, H | F, H | 2 | 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 |
| H | F, G | G | F, G | 2 | 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 |
| I | A, D | nobody | A, D | 2 | 2 ÷ 8 = 0.25 |

: Contacts and node density of each student. {#tbl-apA-contacts-en}

Two cases help to clarify the difference between arrows, choices and
contacts. Student A chooses B and C and is chosen by B, C, D and I; in
the sociogram six arrows touch A, but those linking A to B and to C are
double, so, combining without repeats, there are four contacts: B, C, D
and I. Student D was chosen only once, by I, but has three contacts,
because D also chose A and C: contacts count connections in both
directions, whereas choices received only count those that arrive.

### Step 3: distances and closeness {#sec-apA-step3-en}

To find a student's distances to all classmates, proceed in layers: the
student's contacts are 1 step away; the contacts of those not yet
counted are 2 steps away; and so on, until all eight classmates are
reached. The direction of the arrows is ignored.

For student C, the process is as follows:

1. At 1 step are C's contacts: A, B, D and E.
2. At 2 steps are their contacts not yet counted: I, through A or D,
   and F, through E.
3. At 3 steps are F's contacts not yet counted: G and H.

The sum of the distances is 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 = 14, and C's
closeness is 8 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.57.

Repeating the process for each student gives the distance table
(@tbl-apA-distances-en). Each row gives the distances from one student
to the others; the table is symmetric, because the direction of the
arrows does not count.

| | A | B | C | D | E | F | G | H | I | Sum | Closeness |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:---:|:---------:|
| **A** | − | 1 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 1 | 17 | 8 ÷ 17 ≈ 0.47 |
| **B** | 1 | − | 1 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 2 | 19 | 8 ÷ 19 ≈ 0.42 |
| **C** | 1 | 1 | − | 1 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 3 | 2 | 14 | 8 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.57 |
| **D** | 1 | 2 | 1 | − | 2 | 3 | 4 | 4 | 1 | 18 | 8 ÷ 18 ≈ 0.44 |
| **E** | 2 | 2 | 1 | 2 | − | 1 | 2 | 2 | 3 | 15 | 8 ÷ 15 ≈ 0.53 |
| **F** | 3 | 3 | 2 | 3 | 1 | − | 1 | 1 | 4 | 18 | 8 ÷ 18 ≈ 0.44 |
| **G** | 4 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 1 | − | 1 | 5 | 24 | 8 ÷ 24 ≈ 0.33 |
| **H** | 4 | 4 | 3 | 4 | 2 | 1 | 1 | − | 5 | 24 | 8 ÷ 24 ≈ 0.33 |
| **I** | 1 | 2 | 2 | 1 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 5 | − | 23 | 8 ÷ 23 ≈ 0.35 |

: Distances between the students, in steps, with the sum and the closeness of each one. {#tbl-apA-distances-en}

The smaller the sum, the closer the student is to everyone and the
higher their closeness. G, H and I are at the edges of the network: they
need up to five steps to reach a classmate.

### Step 4: betweenness {#sec-apA-step4-en}

Leaving out the student, the other eight classmates form
8 × 7 ÷ 2 = 28 pairs; each pair counts once, because the pair A-B is the
same as the pair B-A. To avoid missing any, the pairs are laid out in a
**pair grid**:

1. The rows and the columns list the eight classmates, without the
   student being analysed.
2. Only the upper half of the grid, above the diagonal, is filled in:
   7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 28 cells, one per pair.
3. Each cell gets 1 if the shortest path between the two goes through
   the student, ½ if there are two shortest paths and only one goes
   through the student, and 0 if it does not.
4. Betweenness is the sum of the cells divided by 28.

To decide each cell, it helps to cover the student in the sociogram and
see who becomes separated from whom.

For student E, covering E splits the network into {A, B, C, D, I} and
{F, G, H}. Any pair with one classmate on each side has to go through E
and is worth 1: these are rows A, B, C and D in columns F, G and H
(12 cells) and column I in rows F, G and H (3 cells). The remaining
pairs reach each other without E and are worth 0
(@tbl-apA-grid-E-en).

|   | A | B | C | D | F | G | H | I |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **A** | — | 0 | 0 | 0 | **1** | **1** | **1** | 0 |
| **B** |   | — | 0 | 0 | **1** | **1** | **1** | 0 |
| **C** |   |   | — | 0 | **1** | **1** | **1** | 0 |
| **D** |   |   |   | — | **1** | **1** | **1** | 0 |
| **F** |   |   |   |   | — | 0 | 0 | **1** |
| **G** |   |   |   |   |   | — | 0 | **1** |
| **H** |   |   |   |   |   |   | — | **1** |
| **I** |   |   |   |   |   |   |   | — |

: Pair grid for student E. The sum of the cells is 12 + 3 = 15, and the betweenness is 15 ÷ 28 ≈ 0.54. {#tbl-apA-grid-E-en}

For student C, covering C splits the network into {A, B, D, I} and
{E, F, G, H}, and the 4 × 4 = 16 pairs with one classmate on each side
are worth 1. There is also the cell B-D, worth ½: between B and D there
are two shortest paths, B-A-D and B-C-D, and only one goes through C
(@tbl-apA-grid-C-en).

|   | A | B | D | E | F | G | H | I |
|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| **A** | — | 0 | 0 | **1** | **1** | **1** | **1** | 0 |
| **B** |   | — | **½** | **1** | **1** | **1** | **1** | 0 |
| **D** |   |   | — | **1** | **1** | **1** | **1** | 0 |
| **E** |   |   |   | — | 0 | 0 | 0 | **1** |
| **F** |   |   |   |   | — | 0 | 0 | **1** |
| **G** |   |   |   |   |   | — | 0 | **1** |
| **H** |   |   |   |   |   |   | — | **1** |
| **I** |   |   |   |   |   |   |   | — |

: Pair grid for student C. The sum of the cells is 16 + ½ = 16.5, and the betweenness is 16.5 ÷ 28 ≈ 0.59. {#tbl-apA-grid-C-en}

For the other students, the same grid is quick to fill in thanks to
three observations.

**Grids with only zeros.** If all of a student's contacts are connected
to each other, nobody needs to go through that student, because there
is always an equally short or shorter path that avoids them. This
applies to B, whose contacts are A and C; to G, with F and H; to H, with
F and G; and to I, with A and D. The betweenness of these four students
is 0.

**The bridge F.** Covering F separates {A, B, C, D, E, I} from {G, H},
so 6 × 2 = 12 cells are worth 1 and the betweenness is
12 ÷ 28 ≈ 0.43.

**The halves of A and D.** To go from I to C, E, F, G or H there are
always two equally short paths, one through A and the other through D
(for example, I-A-C and I-D-C). These five cells are worth ½ in both
grids.

- In A's grid, the cell B-I is worth 1, because the only shortest path
  is B-A-I; the cell B-D is worth ½ (B-A-D or B-C-D); and the five
  cells with I are worth ½ each, that is, 2.5. The sum is
  1 + ½ + 2.5 = 4, and the betweenness is 4 ÷ 28 ≈ 0.14.
- In D's grid, only the five cells with I have a value, ½ each. The
  sum is 2.5, and the betweenness is 2.5 ÷ 28 ≈ 0.09.

### What the results show {#sec-apA-conclusions-en}

Read together, the values in @tbl-apA-answers-en support a few
conclusions:

- A and C are the most chosen students, with four choices each, and
  the ones with the most contacts.
- C is the most central in betweenness and closeness: C sits in the
  middle of the network, a few steps from everyone, and connects the
  larger group to E.
- E has only two contacts, but comes second in betweenness and
  closeness: without E, the two groups would be disconnected. Being
  popular and acting as a bridge are different positions in a network.
- I was chosen by nobody, but is not isolated: I has two contacts,
  because I chose A and D.
